svg.aria-label: Diagram: how a saga's compensation path works in AWS Step Functions and where it fails. A forward path runs three steps, reserve stock, charge card and book courier, each with its own compensating action. When a step reports an error, Step Functions applies any matching retrier first, and only if the retry policy fails to resolve the error does it transition to the matching catcher. The retrier defaults are shown: IntervalSeconds of 1, MaxAttempts of 3, and a BackoffRate that increases by 2.0, with JitterStrategy defaulting to NONE, and a note that retries are treated as state transitions and therefore billed. The centre of the diagram records the defect that breaks compensation: a catcher's ResultPath determines what input is passed to the compensating state, and if it is not specified it defaults to a dollar sign, which overwrites the entire input, so the compensation arrives holding an error Cause string where the order, payment and reservation identifiers used to be. Setting ResultPath to dollar sign dot error instead adds the error and preserves the input. A lower panel records two gaps in coverage: States.ALL must appear alone in a catcher and cannot catch States.DataLimitExceeded or Runtime errors, and a States.Runtime error is never retriable and always fails the execution, while States.TaskFailed matches any known error except States.Timeout. A final panel records that catchers exist for Task, Parallel and Map states but not for top-level state machine execution failures, so a saga that times out as a whole runs no compensation at all unless the work is nested in a child workflow or a TIMED_OUT event is wired to an external handler.
svg.title: The compensation runs, and arrives holding the error instead of the order
svg.text: The orchestration was never the hard part
Retry asks whether it will work next time. Catch asks what to do now that it will not.
Forward path
1 · Reserve stock
2 · Charge card
3 · Book courier — fails
Retriers run first
IntervalSeconds 1 · MaxAttempts 3 · BackoffRate 2.0
AWS’s example, interval 3: retries at 3s, 6s, 12s.
JitterStrategy defaults to NONE.
“Retries are treated as state transitions” — and billed as them.
then the catcher transitions
“If the retry policy fails to resolve the error,
Step Functions applies the matching catcher.”
→ compensate: refund, release stock
The transition is correct. What it carries may not be.
What the compensation is handed — one setting decides it
no ResultPath → defaults to "$"
Overwrites the entire input. Only the error survives.
"ResultPath": "$.error"
Adds the error, keeps the order and payment ids.
States.ALL is not all
Cannot catch States.DataLimitExceeded, and:
“A retry or catch on States.ALL won’t catch
States.Runtime errors.”
States.TaskFailed matches all but States.Timeout.
The workflow’s own failure has no catcher
Catchers are for “Task, Parallel and Map states, but
not for top-level state machine execution failures.”
A saga that times out compensates nothing.
Nest it in a child workflow, or catch TIMED_OUT.
Compensation is not rollback. Releasing stock is an inverse; a refund leaves both entries on the statement; a sent email has no inverse at all.
Order the steps so the reversible ones run first — and note that a saga with ResultPath set and one without draw the same graph.
